sentences: We like to believe that we are the masters of our tools: that we design them to serve our purposes, and that they remain mere instruments at our disposal.
This reassuring view is only half the truth.
For while we shape our tools, they, in turn, shape us.

The use of a technique is never without effect on the one who employs it; as we use our instruments, they alter our ways of perceiving, thinking, and acting, until they insensibly transform who we are.
This reciprocity is one of the most important, yet most overlooked, truths about our relationship with technology.
Let’s take an ancient example to measure the depth of the phenomenon.
The invention of writing was not just a simple addition of a memory tool; it transformed thought itself.
By allowing ideas to be fixed, reread, compared, and critiqued, it made possible forms of reasoning, analysis, and knowledge accumulation that did not exist in purely oral cultures.
Writing did not merely preserve thought; it changed it, giving rise to a new type of mind.
Moreover, the thinkers of the time feared that it would weaken memory — which it undoubtedly did, while also opening up other possibilities.
Every major tool operates this way: it gives and it takes away, it opens up new capacities while atrophying others.
What writing illustrates over millennia, our contemporary techniques produce before our eyes, at an accelerated pace.

The instruments that allow us to find everything instantly modify our memory and attention; those that connect us constantly transform our relationship with others and with ourselves; those that guide us everywhere alter our sense of direction and space.
Each of these tools provides a real service, but each also transforms us, developing some of our capacities while allowing others to atrophy.
We do not emerge unscathed from the use of our instruments; we emerge changed.
This transformation is all the more profound because it is invisible and involuntary.
We do not decide to be transformed by our tools; this happens without our knowledge, through repeated use, habit, and adaptation.
We believe we remain the same simply by using more efficient instruments, while in reality, these instruments reshape our mental habits, expectations, and ways of being.
The danger lies not in the tools themselves, but in our ignorance of their transformative power, which subjects us to these changes without our perceiving or choosing them.
One does not distrust what one is unaware of the effects of.
Should we conclude that we must renounce our tools, or fear them?
Not at all.

Transformation through technology is not inherently bad; it is the very condition of the human adventure, which has been built by equipping itself with instruments that have each time metamorphosed it.
Humanity is that being who transforms itself by transforming its tools, and there is no going back to a 'pure' humanity that existed before its techniques.
The problem is not that tools change us, but that we are unaware of it, and that we undergo these changes without evaluating them.

What this reciprocity demands is vigilance: to become aware that our tools shape us, to ask how they transform us, which capacities they develop and which they atrophy, and what kind of beings they make of us.
This awareness is not enough to fully control their effects, but it at least allows us to perceive, weigh, and sometimes correct them.
Consciously choosing our tools, measuring what they do to us, deliberately preserving the capacities they tend to erase: this is what a free use of technology entails.
For we cannot prevent our tools from transforming us; but we can, if we are careful, have a say in what they make of us.

sentences: The ecological debate is often framed as a heartbreaking dilemma: to preserve the planet, we would have to give up our comfort, our way of life, and what makes our existence enjoyable.
On one side, the survival of our environment; on the other, the comfort we cherish.

Framed this way, the dilemma seems unsolvable, as it pits two equally valued things against each other, often leading to paralysis: between the planet and comfort, most people actually choose immediate comfort while vaguely worrying about the planet.
However, this framing itself deserves to be questioned, as it may not be as inevitable as it seems.
First, let's acknowledge the truth in the dilemma.
It would be dishonest to claim that preserving our environment will require no change, no sacrifices, or no questioning of certain habits.
Our way of life in wealthy societies heavily impacts ecological balances, and maintaining it as it is simply isn't sustainable.
Those who promise that we can preserve everything without changing anything, that technology will solve everything effortlessly, are nurturing a comfortable but false illusion.
Some renunciation of unsustainable forms of comfort will be necessary, and denying this would be self-deception.
But the dilemma, as it is presented, contains several traps that need to be uncovered.
The first is confusing comfort with a particular, historically situated way of life, which is only one form of it.
What we call 'comfort'—abundant consumption, speed, accumulation—is not the only possible comfort, nor perhaps the greatest.
Other forms of well-being exist that weigh less on the planet: the comfort of slowness, relationships, free time, and a healthy environment.

Pitting the planet against comfort assumes there is only one form of comfort, the one that destroys; it forgets that giving up that kind of comfort could open the door to other forms of well-being, equally real.
The second trap is ignoring that the way of life presented as a comfort to preserve also has its costs, nuisances, and dissatisfactions.
Unrestrained consumption does not bring the happiness it promises; speed is exhausting; accumulation does not fulfill.
A part of what we call comfort is actually a tiring race, a sustained dissatisfaction, a form of alienation.
Giving up this false comfort would not only be a sacrifice for the planet; it could also be a liberation for ourselves.
The dilemma assumes that our current way of life is a pure good that we would only regret giving up; it forgets all that is burdensome about it.
The third trap, finally, is ignoring the costs of inaction, which make the dilemma misleading.

For doing nothing to preserve our comfort does not preserve our comfort: it condemns it, in the long run, to the consequences of ecological destruction, which precisely threaten this way of life and much more.
The real dilemma is not between comfort and the planet, but between a chosen change now and a forced collapse later.
Presenting inaction as maintaining comfort ignores that inaction also leads, and much more surely, to the loss of the comfort it claims to preserve.
Therefore, escaping the false dilemma does not mean denying all renunciation, but rejecting the framing that simply opposes the planet to comfort.

It is to recognize that some sacrifices are necessary, but that they can open up to other forms of well-being; that the way of life to preserve has its own costs; and that inaction preserves nothing but leads to the loss of everything.
The question is not 'should we sacrifice our comfort for the planet?', but 'what kind of life do we want that is both sustainable and desirable?'
Reformulated this way, the question no longer invites paralysis from the dilemma, but the invention of a good life that does not destroy its own conditions.
This is a task more difficult than a simple sacrifice, but also more fruitful: not giving up happiness to save the planet, but rethinking happiness so that it is compatible with it.

sentences: Politics and lying seem inseparable.

Those who believe their leaders are sincere are considered naive, and experience seems to support cynicism: unfulfilled promises, hidden truths, and misleading presentations are the common lot of political life.
This association between governing and lying is so entrenched that it is seen as a fatality: politics would, by nature, be the realm of lies.
But this resignation deserves to be questioned.
Is lying really inherent to the exercise of power, or is it a corruption that we would be wrong to consider inevitable?
We must first recognize what makes sincerity difficult, even problematic, in the exercise of power.

Governing requires dealing with constraints that the ordinary citizen is unaware of; the leader knows things that cannot be disclosed without causing harm, must balance conflicting interests, and cannot always say everything without compromising the action itself.
There is a difference between lying and legitimate reserve: a leader cannot reveal everything, and demanding that would be naive.
Some truths, revealed at the wrong time, would do more harm than good; secrecy, in certain matters, is not a lie but a necessity of action.
Moreover, democratic life itself exerts pressure towards a form of concealment.
A leader who would tell the whole truth — the real difficulties, necessary compromises, inevitable sacrifices — would face an electorate that often prefers pleasant promises to unpleasant truths.
Democracy, by subjecting leaders to the popular verdict, encourages them to flatter rather than tell the truth, to promise more than they can keep, and to hide what would be displeasing.
In a sense, political lying also responds to a demand: that of an audience that does not like to hear difficult truths.
As voters, we have our share in the lies we blame on our leaders.
Should we conclude that lying is a necessity of politics, and that we would be wrong to be indignant about it?
That would be going too far and confusing legitimate reserve with outright lying.

For there is an essential difference between not saying everything and asserting falsehoods, between necessary secrecy and deliberate deception, between withholding what must be withheld and lying about what should be known.
The former can be legitimate; the latter corrupts the bond of trust without which no democracy can function.
It is one thing not to reveal a state secret; it is another to deceive citizens about what underpins their choices, to lie to them to gain or maintain power.
For political lying, in the strong sense, is not just a moral fault; it is an assault on the very foundation of democracy.
Democracy assumes that citizens decide with full knowledge; deceiving them vitiates their decision, making them choose based on false information, thus corrupting the democratic process itself.
A systematically deceived people does not truly govern itself; it believes it is deciding while decisions are being made for it by manipulating what it knows.
Political lying is therefore not a minor sin of public life; it is a corruption of democracy, depriving citizens of the truth they need to govern themselves.
The answer to the question is neither the cynicism that sees lying as inevitable nor the naivety that would demand total transparency.
It is about distinguishing what, in power, falls under legitimate reserve and what falls under corrupting deception, and holding the latter as unacceptable even if the former is necessary.
One can govern without lying, in the sense that one can govern without deliberately deceiving citizens about what underpins their choices, even if one cannot govern by saying everything.

The cynicism that confuses the two, that absolves lying in the name of the necessity of secrecy, does a disservice to democracy: it disarms the demand for truth without which power is held to nothing.
Demanding the truth from those who govern us is not naive; it is defending the very condition of our power as citizens.

sentences: A stretch of sea separates Great Britain from the continent, so narrow that it can be crossed in a few hours, yet so decisive that it has shaped two profoundly different relationships with the world.
British insularity and France's continental position are not mere geographical facts; they have become temperaments, ways of relating to others, almost destinies.
Understanding how geography has transformed into collective psychology sheds light on many differences between the two neighbors, as well as many misunderstandings that separate them.
Insularity has left a lasting imprint on Great Britain.
Being an island means being both connected and separated, open to the sea and protected by it.

This position has fostered a particular relationship with the continent: a distance, a reserve, the feeling of being apart, of not merging with that continental whole to which one is close but not part of.

History has reinforced this feeling: protected by the sea, Great Britain escaped the invasions that ravaged the continent, developed its institutions with relative continuity, and could stay clear of continental upheavals while intervening at will.
Insularity has nurtured a self-awareness as a distinct entity, neither entirely inside nor entirely outside.
France's continental position has produced a completely different relationship with the world.
Rooted in a continent it shares with many neighbors, France has a history made up of contacts, conflicts, and ongoing exchanges with those neighbors, without the protection of a sea.

This position has fostered a more continental awareness, a sense of belonging to a whole of which one is a part, a history where land borders have had to be constantly defended, disputed, and redrawn.

Where insularity protects and separates, continentality exposes and connects; it shapes a relationship with the world where one is necessarily engaged among others, without the distance that the sea provides.
These two positions have shaped different relationships to openness and sovereignty.

British insularity has fostered both a remarkable openness to the sea — towards the vast maritime expanse, towards the world beyond Europe — and a reluctance towards continental engagement, a jealous attachment to a sovereignty that the sea seemed to guarantee.

French continentality, on the other hand, has fostered an assumed continental engagement, the feeling that France's destiny is played out on the continent, among its neighbors, in shared constructions.

These opposing dispositions have weighed, and still weigh, on each one's relationship to the idea of a united Europe, with one engaging in it as if it were its natural space, while the other distrusts it as a dilution of what the sea had preserved.
It would be a mistake to treat these dispositions as mechanical fatalisms, as if geography determined everything.
Peoples are not prisoners of their position; they interpret it, live it, and make choices.
But it would be equally naive to deny that geography has had an impact, that being an island or being continental has shaped lasting ways of relating to others.
The collective psychology of a people is not inscribed in its soil, but it is formed in dialogue with it, in the way a history is written on a given territory.
Insularity and continentality are not imposed destinies, but conditions that have guided, without entirely determining, two relationships to the world.
Understanding this difference in position means understanding many misunderstandings between the two neighbors.

Where the continental sees in the insular reserve selfishness, withdrawal, and a reluctance to engage, the insular sees in continental engagement a threat to a sovereignty that the sea has taught him to cherish.
Neither is simply wrong; they speak from different positions, shaped by a different relationship to the sea and the land.

Measuring this means stopping judging the other from one's own position as if it were the only legitimate one, to understand that each looks at the world from a place that has shaped their perspective.
A stretch of sea, indeed, can separate more deeply than an ocean when it has shaped two ways of being in the world.

sentences: There are words that, it is said, cannot be translated: terms specific to a language, with no exact equivalent in any other, laden with a nuance, a resonance, an experience that other languages cannot convey in a single word.
People enjoy collecting these untranslatable words as revealing curiosities, seeing in them proof that each language carries a unique world, a distinctive way of slicing and experiencing life.
But what exactly is the untranslatable?
Does it really exist, or is it just a surmountable difficulty?
And what does it teach us about the relationships between languages, cultures, and the thoughts they embody?
First, let us acknowledge the reality of the phenomenon.
It is true that some words condense, in a single expression, a nuance that another language can only convey through a periphrase, an approximation, or an elaboration.

These words are not untranslatable in the sense that nothing can be said about them in another language, but in the sense that no single word offers an exact equivalent, where their translation requires an explanation, a paraphrase, and loses along the way the conciseness, resonance, and clarity they had in their original language.
The untranslatable is not the unspeakable; it is what cannot be expressed in a single word, what requires, to move from one language to another, a work that alters its form, if not its meaning.
This untranslatable reveals something profound about languages.

Each language, indeed, has lexicalized certain experiences, certain nuances, certain relationships to the world, while neglecting others; it has forged words for what mattered to the culture that speaks it, and left unnamed what mattered less.

The untranslatables of a language are thus like traces of what a culture deemed worthy of being named with a specific word, revealing its concerns, its sensitivity, and its unique relationship to existence.

That a language has a unique word for a particular nuance of melancholy, a certain form of conviviality, a specific relationship to time or to others, speaks volumes about what matters in the culture that created it.
The untranslatable words are windows into the soul of peoples.
But one must be careful not to draw excessive conclusions from the untranslatable.
Some would see it as proof that cultures are impermeable, incommunicable worlds, that what one language expresses would forever remain inaccessible to others.
This conclusion is false, and the experience of translation disproves it.

For while untranslatables resist word-for-word translation, they do not resist understanding: one can explain them, paraphrase them, make them felt, and someone learning a foreign language eventually comes to understand and even feel those nuances that their own language did not name.
The untranslatable is not the incomprehensible; it is what requires, to be conveyed, more than a mere substitution of words — an effort of understanding that crosses the boundaries of languages.
Here lies the fruitful paradox of translation.

To translate is never merely to mechanically substitute the words of one language for those of another; it is to convey a meaning, an experience, a thought, from one linguistic world to another, at the cost of inevitable losses and equally inevitable discoveries.
The translator cannot render everything; they must choose, sacrifice, compensate, and recreate.
But what they cannot convey in one word, they can make understood in another way; and through their work, what seemed confined to one language becomes accessible to another.

Translation is the living proof that the untranslatable, while complicating the passage from one language to another, does not prohibit it; it is the bridge thrown over the boundaries that untranslatables seemed to erect.
Thus, the untranslatable teaches us a double truth, apparently contradictory yet coherent.

On one hand, languages are not mere interchangeable nomenclatures, designating the same things with different words; each carries a world, a sensitivity, a unique way of articulating experience, of which the untranslatables are witnesses.
On the other hand, these worlds are not impermeable; they communicate, translate, and enrich each other, and anyone learning a foreign language gains access to a world that was not their own.

The untranslatable is therefore not a wall, but a threshold: what, resisting easy translation, invites the effort to understand the other in their uniqueness — and rewards that effort with access to a way of being in the world that no translation could fully deliver, but which the learning of the language ultimately opens up.

sentences: In the face of suffering — whether one's own or that of others — a question arises, as old as humanity itself: does it have meaning?
Does this pain, this ordeal, this misfortune mean anything, serve any purpose, fit into an order that justifies it, or is it pure evil, absurd and gratuitous?
The answer we give to this question is not trivial, as it shapes how we bear suffering and how we view it in others.
Yet it is a daunting question, where consolation borders on deception, and where hasty answers can add to the pain.
The need to find meaning in suffering is profound, and it has fueled countless attempts.
It has been said that suffering purifies, that it elevates, that it teaches, that it redeems, that it prepares for a greater good, that it is part of a design that transcends us.

These answers have consoled many beings, allowing them to bear the unbearable by finding meaning in it; and it would be cruel to dismiss them, as they address a real need — the need to not suffer in vain.
Finding meaning in one's suffering can be what enables one to endure it, to not sink, to continue living.
The meaning attributed to pain can be a strength, a legitimate consolation.
And yet, these answers carry a danger, and sometimes a deception.

For to claim that all suffering has meaning, that it serves a purpose, that it fits into a justifying order, is to risk justifying the unjustifiable, to give meaning to what has none, to add to the pain the lie of false consolation.

In the face of an innocent's suffering, in the presence of gratuitous pain, in the misfortune that teaches nothing and redeems nothing, to claim to find meaning can be an insult, a way of denying the reality of evil, making it acceptable to avoid fighting against it.
There are sufferings that have no meaning, that are pure evil, and to claim otherwise is sometimes less about consolation than about betrayal.
We must therefore distinguish between two gestures that the need for meaning tends to confuse.

One consists of finding, in hindsight, a meaning to a suffering one has endured: saying that an ordeal has made us grow, taught us something, transformed us, is sometimes true, and attributing this meaning to one's own past suffering can be legitimate and fruitful.

The other consists of asserting that all suffering has, in itself, meaning, that it is justified, willed, necessary; and this gesture is much more problematic, as it justifies evil, makes it acceptable, and absolves one from indignation.

That I can, retrospectively, derive meaning from my own ordeal does not mean that suffering is, in itself, meaningful; and generalizing the first gesture into the second is to slide from consolation into deception.

The most accurate position is perhaps the most difficult: to recognize that suffering, in itself, has no given meaning, that it is often pure evil, gratuitous and unjustifiable, and to refuse to justify it with a meaning that would absolve it; and yet to admit that we can, sometimes, give meaning to our suffering, not by justifying it, but by transforming it, by drawing from the endured ordeal something that places it in our history without making it acceptable.
The meaning of suffering is not in suffering itself; it is, if it exists, in what we make of it, in the response we provide.
Suffering means nothing by itself; but we can, in the face of it, create meaning — not by justifying it, but by refusing to let it have the final word.
This distinction has a decisive ethical consequence.
For if suffering has no meaning in itself, then it should not be accepted, justified, sanctified; it must be fought against.

The temptation to give meaning to suffering can lead to a guilty resignation, to accepting evil as if it were justified; refusing this meaning, recognizing that suffering is gratuitous evil, gives us the means to combat it rather than resigning ourselves to it.
In the face of the suffering of others, in particular, our first duty is not to find a comforting meaning for them, but to relieve it, to combat it, to refuse its existence.
True respect for the one who suffers is not to explain the meaning of their pain, but to take it seriously as an evil, and to do what is in our power to put an end to it.
Suffering may not have meaning; but our response to it does.

sentences: What distinguishes the creative genius from the mere skilled individual, the one who produces truly new works from the one who correctly applies the recipes of his art?
This question, which touches on the mystery of creation, engages the relationship between genius and rule.
For art has its rules, its techniques, its traditions; and yet, the great creator seems to escape the rule, transgress it, invent.
Should we conclude that genius is the opposite of rule, that it creates by freeing itself from all norms?
Or is its relationship to rule more subtle?
To probe this question is to approach the mystery of what makes a true creator.
A first conception, romantic in nature, opposes genius to rule.

Genius would be the one who, through a creative force that comes from who knows where, frees himself from established rules, breaks traditions, and invents freely, without being bound by the norms of his art.
This conception has its allure: it makes the creator an exceptional being, a force of nature, whose originality lies precisely in the rejection of rules.
And it captures a part of the truth: great creators have often transgressed the rules of their time, invented new forms, and broken with established traditions.
Genius does not merely apply the rules; it surpasses them, creating what no rule anticipated.
But this conception, taken alone, is misleading, as it overlooks the profound relationship of genius to rule.
The great creator does not free himself from rules out of ignorance or ease; he first masters them, perfectly, before surpassing them.
One only transgresses fruitfully what one knows intimately; the genius who invents new forms has first assimilated the old forms, mastered the tradition, and possessed the rules of his art.
His freedom regarding the rules is not that of the ignorant who ignores them, but that of the master who has assimilated them so well that he can surpass them.
Genius is not the absence of rule, but its mastery so complete that it allows one to go beyond.
There is more.
Genius does not merely transgress the old rules; it invents new ones.
The brilliant work, which initially seems to escape all rules, reveals upon examination a necessity, a coherence, a law of its own, which was not that of the old rules but is nonetheless a law.
The creator does not do just anything; he invents a new way of doing, which has its rigor, its necessity, and which will in turn become a rule, a model, a tradition.
What appeared as transgression reveals itself as foundation; the genius who breaks the old rules establishes new ones, opening paths that others will follow.

A thinker has said that genius is the one who gives rules to art, not the one who receives them: he does not follow pre-existing rules, but his work sets the rule, becomes the model from which others will derive norms.
This conception sheds light on the dialectical relationship between genius and tradition.

The true creator is neither the pure conservative who applies received rules, nor the pure rebel who rejects them all; he is the one who, having assimilated tradition, extends it by transforming it, surpassing it by drawing from it.

There is a continuity even in the rupture: genius is inscribed within a tradition that it transforms, dialogues with its predecessors whom it surpasses, invents the new from the heritage it has made its own.
True creation is neither repetition nor a clean slate; it is a fruitful transformation of a heritage, an invention that extends by surpassing.
Understanding the relationship between genius and rule has implications that go beyond aesthetics, as it applies to all creation, in all fields.

In science, in thought, in all art, the true creator is the one who, having mastered the achievements of his field, knows how to surpass them, inventing anew without starting from nothing, transforming tradition rather than repeating or rejecting it.
This lesson also applies to those who learn: for mastering the rules first, deeply assimilating them, is the condition for one day being able to surpass them.
One does not create by ignoring the rules, but by possessing them so well that one can go beyond.
Genius is not the opposite of mastery; it is its fulfillment, the point where the complete mastery of the rules finally allows one to transcend them.
There is no creative freedom without the prior mastery from which it frees itself—and this may be the highest lesson about what it means to learn, in art as in everything.

sentences: There is a question about the nature of goodness that has long divided moral thought: is true goodness spontaneous or costly?

Must we, in order to be truly good, have goodness come naturally to us, to do it effortlessly, by inclination; or does true moral value, on the contrary, require effort, struggle against oneself, victory over one's inclinations?
This question, seemingly subtle, touches on what constitutes the moral value of an act and a being, and the opposing answers reveal two deep conceptions of morality.
One conception sees spontaneous goodness as the highest.
The one who does good naturally, effortlessly, out of a generous inclination, would be truly good; their goodness would be pure, uncalculated, unforced.

In contrast, the one who must struggle against their bad inclinations to do good would reveal, through that very struggle, that they are not truly good, that evil attracts them, and that they only do good by forcing themselves.
According to this view, accomplished virtue is that which has become second nature, which does good with ease, spontaneously, without effort or struggle.
The truly good person would be one for whom doing good is self-evident, who does not have to force themselves, whose goodness flows naturally.
This conception has its strength and beauty; it describes an ideal of accomplished virtue, where goodness has become natural.
But it faces a powerful objection, brought forth by an opposing conception.

For if spontaneous goodness is admirable, it also seems, in a sense, to lack merit: the one who does good naturally, due to a fortunate temperament, has no more merit than one who is born beautiful or intelligent; their goodness is a gift, not a conquest.

Moral merit, from this perspective, requires effort, struggle, victory over oneself: the one who does good by overcoming their contrary inclinations, by fighting against themselves, deserves more, for their goodness is a conquest, not a received gift.
Moral value would lie in effort, not in ease.
These two conceptions seem irreconcilable, yet each captures a part of the truth.

It is true that spontaneous goodness has something admirable about it, that a virtue that has become natural and easy is an accomplishment; it would be strange to prefer a goodness that is always painful, always forced, to a goodness that has become second nature.

But it is also true that effort, struggle, and victory over oneself have their own moral value, that the one who does good despite their contrary inclinations demonstrates a moral strength that the one for whom everything is easy does not have.
How can we reconcile these two truths?
Perhaps by distinguishing two moments in moral life.

At the beginning, goodness is costly: one must struggle against their inclinations, force themselves, conquer within themselves the disposition to do good; this is the time of effort, where moral value is proven in battle.
But this repeated effort can shape a disposition, a habit, a character, where doing good gradually becomes easier, more natural, until it becomes second nature.
The spontaneous goodness of the accomplished person is not then an initial gift, but the fruit of long effort, virtue conquered and made natural through practice.
What was costly becomes easy, not through a received gift, but through a completed conquest.

Thus, the two conceptions reconcile: true goodness is spontaneous, but this spontaneity is the fruit of effort; it is a gift, but a gift that one has given to oneself through the patient conquest of virtue.
This conception has both demanding and encouraging implications.
Demanding, because it refuses to exempt one from effort on the grounds that one might not be naturally good: goodness is conquered, it requires struggle, work on oneself.
Encouraging, because it affirms that this conquest is possible, that repeated effort can shape a character, transform a disposition, make easy what was difficult.
One is not born good, or one is only good to varying degrees; but one can become good through practice, habit, and self-formation.
Goodness is neither a pure gift that one has or does not have, nor a perpetual effort without hope of ease; it is a conquest that, patiently pursued, can become second nature.
Being good without effort is possible, not as a starting point, but as an outcome — the culmination of a long work on oneself that has turned painful goodness into natural goodness.
And perhaps that is the highest answer: that accomplished virtue is that which, having been conquered through effort, has become so much our own that it no longer demands it.

sentences: I believe that too, Marbre," Jasper Hobson simply replied, and he went back into the common room.
However, with the southeast wind, the sky was clearing quickly and the atmosphere was lifting the vapors that had obscured it.
Jasper Hobson could hope, not without reason, that the next day he would be able to take his position.
Indeed, the night was colder, and fine snow fell, covering the entire territory of the island.
In the morning, when he got up, Jasper Hobson was able to greet this first sign of winter.
It was September 2nd.
The sky gradually cleared of the vapors that had been fogging it.
The sun appeared.
The lieutenant was waiting for him.
At noon, he made a good latitude observation, and around two o'clock, a calculation of the hour angle that gave him his longitude.
Thus, despite the violence of the hurricane, the drifting island had more or less maintained its position on the same parallel.
Only, the current had pushed it further west.
At that moment, it was located across from the Bering Strait, but at least four hundred miles north of Cape Oriental and Cape Prince of Wales, which mark the narrowest part of the strait.

sentences: France has a unique relationship with itself, summed up by an expression it cherishes: the French exception.
It likes to see itself as a special case, a nation that is unlike any other, bearing a particular vocation and holding a universal message.
This claim to exceptionality, which foreigners sometimes find arrogant, deserves to be questioned: where does it come from, what does it reveal, what is founded and what is illusory about it?
For it speaks to something profound about France's relationship with itself and the world, its greatness and its blind spots.
Where does this awareness of being an exception come from?
From history, first and foremost.
France has long been a great power, a center of Europe, a hub of cultural and political influence.

It produced a revolution that claimed to carry a universal message, proclaiming rights valid for all men; it saw itself as the homeland of universal ideas, the nation that would speak on behalf of all humanity.

From this history arose a particular consciousness: that of a nation that would not be just another nation, defined solely by its own interests, but one that carries a universal vocation, a message that transcends its borders.
France sees itself less as a particular nation than as the embodiment of the universal.
This claim has its grandeur.
It expresses an aspiration to rise above the narrowness of national interests, to serve universal values, and to speak in the name of humanity rather than just for oneself.
It has inspired generous struggles, a commitment to principles that transcend borders, a generosity that has made France a land of welcome, a refuge, a voice for the oppressed.
This universalist dimension, when it is true to itself, has something noble about it; it rejects self-absorption, national selfishness, and the reduction of politics to mere interests.
France, which sees itself as a bearer of the universal, can be a generous, open country, true to its best qualities.
But this claim also has its illusions and dangers.

The first illusion is to confuse its universal with the universal, to take its own particular values as values valid for all, to impose on others, in the name of the universal, what is merely its own singularity.

Universalism can become a form of arrogance, even imperialism, when it claims that its way of seeing is the only valid one, that other cultures should conform to it, and that what is French would thereby be universal.

France has sometimes succumbed to this temptation, imposing its values in the name of the universal, failing to recognize the legitimacy of other ways of being, and confusing its message with the truth.
The second illusion is the gap between pretension and reality.

Thinking of oneself as an exception, as a great nation carrying a universal message, can obscure a more modest reality, sustain the illusion of a greatness that the facts contradict, and nurture a nostalgia for a role that is no longer one's own.

Present-day France is no longer the power it once was; still thinking of itself as an exception can be a way of not seeing its true place in the world, of living in nostalgia for a past greatness, and of confusing what it was with what it is.
The claim to exception can thus be a form of blindness, a refusal to see its real condition.
What can we conclude from this French singularity?
Perhaps it is, as often, ambivalent: carrying both a greatness and illusions, a noble aspiration and dangerous temptations.
The aspiration to the universal, to transcend the narrowness of interests, to serve values that transcend borders, is what France has at its best, and it would be a shame for it to renounce that.

But it must guard against the illusions that accompany it: confusing its particular with the universal, imposing its singularity on others in the name of humanity, and comforting itself with a greatness that the present contradicts.

The French exception, when well understood, is not the arrogant claim of being superior to others, but the fidelity to a universalist aspiration that, if it remains clear-eyed about its limits, can be a valuable contribution to the world.

Thinking of oneself as an exception can be greatness or blindness; it all depends on the clarity with which one embraces this singularity — as a vocation to serve the universal, not as a right to impose oneself in its name.

sentences: Nothing in excess." This maxim, engraved it is said on the front of an ancient temple, summarizes one of humanity's oldest wisdoms: that of measure, of the right proportion, of moderation.
Avoiding excess, maintaining measure in all things, not falling into too much or too little, this would be the path of wisdom.
Does this venerable wisdom of measure still hold meaning in our time, which seems on the contrary to praise excess, extravagance, and always wanting more?
To question the wisdom of measure is to ask what value this ancient lesson still has today.
The wisdom of measure is based on a deep intuition: that good often lies in a just middle ground between two opposing extremes, and that virtue consists in avoiding both too much and too little.
Courage is a middle ground between cowardice and recklessness; generosity, between stinginess and extravagance; self-confidence, between timidity and arrogance.
In every domain, virtue would be this just measure, this point of balance between opposing extremes, which discernment must find.
This conception, developed by the Ancients, makes measure not a lukewarm mediocrity, but a difficult correctness, a balance to be achieved between easier extremes.
This wisdom extends beyond morality, to the entire art of living.

It teaches not to become excessively attached to external goods, to enjoy them without becoming enslaved to them; not to be swept away by passions, but to master them; to maintain, in both success and trials, a state of equanimity that is neither exalted nor depressed.
Measure is this self-control that refuses to be swept away by excesses, that maintains the right proportion in all things, that preserves inner balance against what would seek to disrupt it.
It is the condition of serenity, of that peace of the soul that excesses disturb and that measure preserves.
Yet our time seems to be the opposite of this wisdom.

It praises excess, always wanting more, and excessiveness; it values intensity, limitless performance, and pushing beyond all boundaries; it scorns moderation as a lukewarmness, mediocrity, and resignation.
Consumer society stirs up limitless desires; the race for performance knows no measure; the demand for intensity disregards balance.
In this context, the wisdom of moderation seems outdated, contrary to the spirit of the times, a virtue of old sages that has fallen out of favor.
Should we conclude that it has lost its meaning, that it belongs to a bygone era?
On the contrary, it may never have been as necessary as it is now.

For the excesses of our time — the excessiveness of consumption, performance, the exploitation of nature, and our technical powers — are precisely what threatens us, exhausts us, and destroys our balance and that of the world.

The ecological crisis is a crisis of excess, of always wanting more; contemporary malaise partly arises from excess, from relentless intensity, from an unmeasured race; the imbalance between our powers and our wisdom is a failure of moderation.
In a world threatened by its own excesses, the wisdom of moderation, far from being outdated, finds a new urgency; it is perhaps what our time needs most.
Rehabilitating the wisdom of moderation is not about advocating for lukewarmness, mediocrity, or giving up on intensity.
It is recognizing that good often lies in the right proportion, that excess destroys what it claims to enhance, and that excess leads to ruin.
It is about rediscovering the sense of limits, balance, and moderation in a world that has lost them.
Moderation is not the enemy of intensity or greatness; it is their condition, for what is without measure destroys itself, while what maintains the right proportion endures and fulfills itself.

"Nothing in excess": this ancient maxim, far from being outdated, perhaps expresses the wisdom that our age of excess most desperately needs — the acknowledgment that everything has its measure, and to exceed it is to court disaster.
In a world intoxicated by excess, rediscovering the sense of moderation may be the beginning of wisdom.

sentences: Sleep is not just a simple break in our day, as one might think.
During the night, our brain actually remains very active and does essential work for our physical and mental health.
Scientists have been studying the complex mechanisms that occur while we sleep for decades.
Sleep is divided into several phases that repeat multiple times during the night.
The first phase is light sleep, during which it is easy to wake up.
Next comes a phase of deep sleep, which is essential for the body's physical recovery.
Finally, a phase called REM sleep corresponds to the time when we dream most intensely.
During deep sleep, the body repairs muscle tissues and strengthens the immune system.
It is also during this phase that growth hormone is produced in larger quantities, which explains why sleep is particularly important for growing children and adolescents.
REM sleep, for its part, plays a crucial role in memory and learning.
Researchers have shown that the brain sorts, during this phase, the information received during the day.
It strengthens important memories and eliminates information deemed unnecessary, much like cleaning up our thoughts.
Several studies have shown the negative consequences of lack of sleep on our bodies.
A person who sleeps poorly for several consecutive nights sees their concentration drop significantly.
Their ability to make decisions and solve problems is also affected.
Lack of sleep is also associated with increased irritability and mood swings.
In the long term, insufficient sleep can have more serious consequences for health.
Research has established a link between chronic lack of sleep and a higher risk of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and weight gain.
The body, deprived of sufficient rest, produces more stress-related hormones, which wears the body out over time.
In light of these findings, sleep specialists recommend that adults sleep between seven and nine hours per night, depending on individual needs.
They also advise avoiding bright screens before going to bed, as blue light disrupts the production of melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleep onset.

Establishing a regular routine, by going to bed and waking up at similar times each day, remains one of the best ways to sustainably improve sleep quality and, consequently, overall health, according to experts.

sentences: On July 6 and 7, we followed the spirals of this fault, penetrating another two leagues into the Earth's crust, which brought us nearly five leagues below sea level.
But on the 8th, around noon, the fault took a much gentler slope in the southeast direction, about forty-five degrees.
The path then became easy and perfectly monotonous.
It was hard to imagine it being any different.
The journey could not be varied by the incidents of the landscape.
Finally, on Wednesday the 15th, we were seven leagues underground and about fifty leagues from Sneffels.
Although we were a bit tired, our health remained reassuring, and the travel pharmacy was still intact.
My uncle kept track hour by hour of the readings from the compass, the chronometer, the manometer, and the thermometer, the very ones he published in the scientific account of his journey.
He could therefore easily assess his situation.
When he told me that we were at a horizontal distance of fifty leagues, I couldn't help but exclaim.
—It's that, if your calculations are correct, we are no longer under Iceland.

sentences: So, there was no longer any doubt that during the storm a gust of wind had occurred, which we had not noticed, and had brought the raft back towards the shores my uncle thought he had left behind.
It would be impossible for me to describe the succession of feelings that stirred Professor Lidenbrock: astonishment, disbelief, and finally, anger.
Never have I seen a man so taken aback at first, and then so irritated.
The fatigue of the crossing, the dangers faced, everything had to start over!
We had gone backwards instead of moving forwards!
Ah!
Fate plays such tricks on me!
he exclaimed; the elements conspire against me!
Air, fire, and water are combining their efforts to oppose my passage!
Well!
we shall see what my will can do.

I will not yield, I will not back down an inch, and we will see who will prevail, man or nature!” Standing on the rock, irritated and threatening, Otto Lidenbrock, like the fierce Ajax, seemed to challenge the gods.
But I thought it wise to intervene and put a stop to this reckless fervor.
“Listen to me,” I said to him in a firm tone.

There is a limit to all ambition here on earth; one must not struggle against the impossible; we are poorly equipped for a sea voyage; five hundred leagues cannot be covered on a poor assembly of beams with a blanket for a sail, a stick for a mast, and against the unleashed winds.
We cannot steer, we are at the mercy of the storms, and it is madness to attempt this impossible crossing a second time!

sentences: But then the Victoria was disappearing far away in the sky.
Joe decided to wait for it: it would certainly come back!
It did come back, indeed, but further east.
Joe ran, gestured, shouted...
It was in vain!
A violent wind was carrying the balloon away with irresistible speed!
For the first time, energy and hope failed the unfortunate man; he saw himself lost; he thought his master had left for good; he no longer dared to think, he no longer wanted to reflect.
Like a madman, with bloody feet and a battered body, he walked all day and part of the night.
He dragged himself along, sometimes on his knees, sometimes on his hands; he could see the moment approaching when he would run out of strength and would have to die.

As he advanced like this, he eventually found himself facing a marsh, or rather what he soon realized was a marsh, since night had fallen a few hours earlier; he unexpectedly fell into thick mud; despite his efforts, despite his desperate resistance, he felt himself sinking gradually into this muddy ground; a few minutes later, he was stuck up to his waist.

sentences: Doctor Fergusson, after taking in the whole scene at a glance, approached the wooden bed of the sovereign.
He saw there a man in his forties, completely stupefied by all sorts of orgies and beyond help.
This illness, which had been dragging on for years, was nothing but a perpetual drunkenness.

This royal drunkard had more or less lost consciousness, and not even all the ammonia in the world could have brought him back to his feet. The favorites and women, kneeling, bowed during this solemn visit.

With a few drops of a strong cordial, the doctor briefly revived this stupefied body; the sultan moved, and for a corpse that had shown no signs of life for several hours, this symptom was met with renewed cries in honor of the doctor.
The doctor, having had enough, quickly brushed aside his overly demonstrative admirers and left the palace.
He headed towards the Victoria.
It was six o'clock in the evening.
Joe, during his absence, was waiting calmly at the bottom of the ladder; the crowd was paying him the utmost respect.
As a true Son of the Moon, he let them do as they pleased.
For a deity, he looked like quite a decent man, not proud, even familiar with the young African women, who never tired of watching him.
He also spoke to them in friendly terms.
"Worship, ladies, worship," he told them; "I am a good fellow, though the son of a goddess!" He was presented with propitiatory gifts, usually placed in the 'mzimu' or fetish huts.
These consisted of ears of barley and 'pombé.' Joe felt obliged to taste this kind of strong beer; however, his palate, though accustomed to gin and whiskey, could not handle its strength.
He made a terrible grimace, which the audience took for a friendly smile.
In front of us stretched four marble steps, and at the bottom of the last step, a boat was gently swaying.
From where we were, we could see a dark mass rising in the middle of a lake; it was the kiosk we were heading to.
That kiosk seemed quite far away to me, perhaps because of the darkness.
We got into the boat.
I remember that the oars made no sound as they touched the water; I leaned over to look at them: they were wrapped with the sashes of our Palicares.
Besides the rowers, there were only women in the boat, my father, my mother, Sélim, and me.
The Palicares had remained on the shore of the lake, kneeling on the last step, forming a barrier with the other three in case they were pursued.
I didn’t understand.
Why was my father fleeing, he who was all-powerful, he before whom others usually fled, he who had taken as his motto: 'Indeed, it was a flight that my father was making across the lake.'
He later told me that the garrison of the castle of Janina, tired from long service....” Here, Haydée fixed her expressive gaze on Monte-Cristo, whose eyes never left hers.
The young girl then continued slowly, like someone who is inventing or omitting.
You were saying, signora, Albert interjected, who was paying the closest attention to this story, that the garrison of Janina, tired from long service.

No, she said, I don’t remember it; but perhaps I will recall it later, and I will say it.
She spent the night like that.
The lamp went out when there was no more oil: she saw neither the darkness nor the light, and day returned without her seeing the day.
The pain had placed a blindfold over her eyes that allowed her to see only Edmond.
Ah!
You are here!
she said at last, turning towards Fernand.
I haven't left you since yesterday," replied Fernand with a painful sigh.

sentences: She felt, moreover, more irritated with him.

He was taking on a heavier appearance with age; he was uncorking empty bottles at dessert; he was running his tongue over his teeth after eating; he made a gurgling sound with each sip of his soup, and as he began to gain weight, his already small eyes seemed to be lifted towards his temples by the swelling of his cheeks.

Sometimes, Emma would tuck the red trim of his sweaters into his vest, adjust his tie, or toss aside the faded gloves he was about to put on; and it wasn't, as he thought, for him; it was for herself, out of a burst of selfishness, a nervous irritation.

Sometimes too, she would talk to him about things she had read, like a passage from a novel, a new play, or the anecdotes of high society that were recounted in the newspaper; for, after all, Charles was someone, always a willing ear, always ready to approve.
She confided a lot in her little dog!
She would have done so with the logs in the fireplace and the pendulum of the clock.
Spring returned.
She experienced breathlessness in the early warmth when the pear trees bloomed.
At the beginning of July, she counted on her fingers how many weeks were left until October, thinking that the Marquis of Andervilliers might still give a ball at Vaubyessard.
But all of September passed without letters or visits.
After the boredom of this disappointment, her heart was once again empty, and then the series of the same days began again.
They were now going to follow one after the other, always the same, countless, and bringing nothing!
Other lives, however dull they might be, at least had the chance of an event.
An adventure sometimes brought endless twists and turns, and the scenery changed.
But for her, nothing happened; God had willed it!
The future was a completely dark corridor, with a tightly shut door at the end.

sentences: In the evening, on his way back, Charles recalled one by one the phrases she had said, trying to remember them and to complete their meaning, in order to grasp the part of her life that she had lived during the time he did not yet know her.
But he could never picture her in his mind any differently than he had seen her the first time, or as he had just left her a moment ago.
Then he wondered what she would become, if she would marry, and to whom?
Alas!
Monsieur Rouault was quite wealthy, and she!...
So beautiful!
But Emma's image always returned to his mind, and something monotonous like the buzzing of a spinning top droned in his ears: "If only you would marry, though!

If only you would marry!" That night, he did not sleep, his throat was tight, he was thirsty; he got up to drink from his water jug and opened the window; the sky was covered with stars, a warm wind was blowing, and in the distance, dogs were barking.
He turned his head towards the Bertaux.

Thinking that after all there was nothing to lose, Charles promised himself he would propose when the opportunity arose; but every time it did, the fear of not finding the right words stuck to his lips.
Monsieur Rouault would not have been upset if someone had taken his daughter off his hands, as she was of little use to him in his home.
He excused her internally, thinking she had too much spirit for farming, a cursed profession from heaven, since one never saw a millionaire in it.

Far from having made a fortune, the old man lost money there every year; for while he excelled in the markets, where he enjoyed the tricks of the trade, the actual farming, with the internal management of the farm, suited him less than anyone.
He was reluctant to take his hands out of his pockets, and he did not spare expenses for anything concerning his life, wanting to be well-fed, well-heated, and well-rested.
He loved strong cider, rare leg of lamb, and long-beaten glorias.
He took his meals in the kitchen, alone, in front of the fire, at a small table that was brought to him fully set, like in a theater.

sentences: One of these silver foxes was a magnificent animal, slightly larger than the common fox.
It had ears, shoulders, and a tail of smoky black, but the fine tip of its tail and the tops of its eyebrows were white.

The particular circumstances in which this fox was killed deserve to be recounted in detail, as they justified certain concerns of Lieutenant Hobson, as well as some defensive precautions he felt he had to take.
On the morning of September 24, two sleds had brought Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, the lieutenant, Sergeant Long, Marbre, and Sabine to Morse Bay.
Fox tracks had been spotted the day before by a few men from the detachment, among rocks where thin shrubs were growing, and certain undeniable signs had revealed their passage.
The hunters, eager for the chase, set out to find a trail that promised them a valuable prize, and indeed, their search was not in vain.
Two hours after their arrival, a rather fine silver fox lay dead on the ground.
Two or three other carnivores were also glimpsed.
The hunters then split up.
While Marbre and Sabine pursued the tracks of one fox, Lieutenant Hobson, Mrs.
Paulina Barnett, and Sergeant Long tried to cut off the retreat of another fine animal that was trying to hide behind the rocks.
It was necessary to be cunning with this fox, which, barely showing itself, exposed no part of its body to the impact of a bullet.
For half an hour, this pursuit continued without yielding any results.
However, the animal was surrounded on three sides, with the sea blocking the fourth.
It soon realized the disadvantage of its situation and decided to escape with a tremendous leap, leaving the hunter with no other chance than to shoot it in mid-air.

sentences: My uncle stomped his foot while the horses headed towards the ferry.
I fully understood the necessity of waiting for a certain moment of the tide to undertake the crossing of the fjord, the moment when the sea, having reached its highest point, is calm.
At that point, the ebb and flow have no noticeable effect, and the ferry is not at risk of being swept away, either to the bottom of the gulf or out into the open ocean.
The favorable moment only arrived at six o'clock in the evening; my uncle, I, the guide, two ferrymen, and the four horses had taken our places in a kind of rather fragile flat-bottomed boat.
Having been used to the steam ferries of the Elbe, I found the oars of the boatmen to be a sad mechanical device.
It took more than an hour to cross the fjord; but finally, the crossing was made without incident.
It should have been dark, but at the sixty-fifth parallel, the daylight of the polar regions should not have surprised me; in Iceland, during the months of June and July, the sun does not set.
Nevertheless, the temperature had dropped; I was cold, and especially hungry.
Welcoming was the 'böer' that opened hospitably to receive us.
It was the house of a peasant, but in terms of hospitality, it was worth that of a king.
Upon our arrival, the host came to shake our hands, and without further ceremony, he signaled for us to follow him.
To follow him, indeed, as accompanying him would have been impossible.

A long, narrow, dark passage led into this dwelling built of barely squared beams and allowed access to each of the rooms; there were four of them: the kitchen, the weaving workshop, the 'badstofa', the family's bedroom, and, the best of all, the guest room.
My uncle, whose height had not been considered when building the house, did not fail to bump his head three or four times against the protrusions of the ceiling.
We were shown into our room, a sort of large hall with a packed earth floor and lit by a window whose panes were made of rather opaque sheep membranes.
The bedding consisted of dry straw thrown into two wooden frames painted red and adorned with Icelandic proverbs.
I did not expect this comfort; however, there was a strong smell of dried fish, cured meat, and sour milk in this house that did not sit well with my sense of smell.

Yes, sir, the count, said Julie; we can say this, for He has done for us what He only does for His chosen ones; He has sent us one of His angels." The color rose to the count's cheeks, and he coughed to find a way to hide his emotion by bringing his handkerchief to his mouth.

Those who are born in a cradle of purple and have never desired anything, said Emmanuel, do not know what it is to experience the joy of living; just as those who have never risked their lives to the mercy of four planks tossed on a raging sea do not know the value of a clear sky." Monte-Cristo stood up, and without responding, for the tremor in his voice would have revealed the emotion he was feeling, he began to pace the salon.
Our magnificence makes you smile, sir, the count, said Maximilien, who was following Monte-Cristo with his eyes.

No, no, replied Monte-Cristo, very pale and pressing one hand against his heart, while with the other he pointed out to the young man a crystal globe under which a silk purse lay precious and resting on a black velvet cushion.

I was just wondering what this purse is for, which seems to contain a paper on one side and a rather beautiful diamond on the other." "This, sir, the count, is the most precious of our family treasures.

sentences: Which of you, gentlemen, asked the magistrate without responding to the count, is named Andrea Cavalcanti?" A cry of astonishment erupted from all corners of the salon.
They searched; they questioned.
A few moments after the scene of confusion that unfolded in Mr. Danglars' salons,

the vast hotel had emptied with a speed comparable to that which would have followed the announcement of a case of plague or cholera among the guests: within minutes, through all the doors, up all the stairs, by every exit, everyone hurried to leave, or rather to flee; for this was one of those situations where one should not even attempt to offer the banal consolations that make the best friends so intrusive in great catastrophes.

Only Danglars remained in the banker’s hotel, locked in his office, giving his statement to the gendarmerie officer; Mrs. Danglars, terrified, in the boudoir we know, and Eugénie, who, with a haughty eye and a disdainful lip, had retreated to her room with her inseparable companion, Miss Louise d'Armilly.

As for the numerous servants, even more numerous that evening than usual, since they had been joined, for the occasion of the party, by the waiters, cooks, and head waiters from the Café de Paris, turning their anger against their masters for what they called their affront, they gathered in groups in the pantry, the kitchens, and their rooms, caring very little about the service, which, in any case, was naturally interrupted.
Amid these various characters, trembling with different interests, only two deserve our attention: Miss Eugénie Danglars and Miss Louise d'Armilly.
The young fiancée, as we mentioned, had withdrawn with a haughty air, a disdainful lip, and the gait of an outraged queen, followed by her companion, who was paler and more agitated than she.
Upon arriving in her room, Eugénie closed her door behind her, while Louise sank into a chair.
"Oh!
my God, my God!
the horrible thing, said the young musician; and who could have suspected this?
Mr.
Andrea Cavalcanti...
an assassin...
a fugitive from prison...
a convict!"

The enormous shell was brought to the top of Stone's Hill.

It was an exhilarating moment.

sentences: Master Mac Nap first went to choose the trees needed for his construction.
He found a large number of these pines on the hills that closely resemble Scots pine.
These trees were of medium height and very suitable for the house he was to build.
In these rough dwellings, indeed, walls, floors, ceilings, partition walls, beams, ridge beams, rafters, shingles, everything consists of planks, beams, and girders.
It is understandable that this type of construction requires only very basic labor, and Mac Nap was able to proceed quickly — which in no way affected the solidity of the dwelling.
Master Mac Nap chose straight trees, which were cut a foot above the ground.
These pines, stripped of branches, numbering around a hundred, neither barked nor squared, formed as many girders each twenty feet long.
The axe and the adze only touched their ends to carve the tenons and mortises that would fix them to one another.
This operation took only a few days to complete, and soon all these woods, dragged by dogs, were transported to the plateau where the main house was to be located.
Previously, this plateau had been carefully leveled.
The ground, mixed with soil and fine sand, was beaten and compacted with heavy pounding.

The short grasses and the sparse shrubs that covered it had been burned on the spot, and the ashes resulting from the incineration formed a thick layer on the surface, completely impermeable to any moisture.
In this way, Mac Nap obtained a clean and dry site on which he could safely establish his first interconnections.
With this first work completed, at each corner of the house and directly above the partition walls, the main beams rose vertically, which were to support the frame of the house.
They were driven a few feet into the ground after their ends had been hardened in the fire.
These beams, slightly hollowed out on their side faces, received the transverse girders of the actual wall, between which the openings for doors and windows had been previously made.
At their upper part, these beams were joined by ties that, being well fitted into the mortises, thus consolidated the entire structure.
These ties represented the entablature of the two facades, and it was at their ends that the high roof trusses rested, whose lower ends overhung the wall, like the roof of a chalet.
On the square of the entablature, the ceiling girders extended, and on the layer of ashes, those of the floor.

sentences: Since Franz still had enough time to catch up with his companion, and he no longer had to worry about his accommodation in Rome, he accepted this proposal to make up for his first hunt.
Upon his affirmative response, the sailors exchanged a few low words among themselves.
--No, the captain replied; but we must inform Your Excellency that the island is in default.

--That means that, since Monte-Cristo is uninhabited and sometimes serves as a stopover for smugglers and pirates coming from Corsica, Sardinia, or Africa, if any sign reveals our stay on the island, we will be forced, upon our return to Livorno, to undergo a quarantine of six days.
--Devil!
That certainly changes the thesis!
Six days!
Just as long as it took God to create the world.
That's a bit long, my children.
The captain commanded the maneuver; they set course for the island, and the boat began to sail in that direction.

Franz let the operation finish, and when they had taken the new route, when the sail had filled with the breeze, and the four sailors had taken their places, three at the front and one at the helm, he resumed the conversation.
"My dear Gaetano," he said to the captain, "you just told me, I believe, that the island of Monte-Cristo served as a refuge for pirates, which seems to me to be quite a different game than goats.
I was well aware of the existence of smugglers, but I thought that since the capture of Algiers and the destruction of the Regency, pirates only existed in the novels of Cooper and Captain Marryat.
Well, Your Excellency is mistaken: pirates are like bandits, who are supposed to have been exterminated by Pope Leo XII, yet they still stop travelers every day at the gates of Rome.
Haven't you heard that barely six months ago, the French chargé d'affaires near the Holy See was robbed just five hundred paces from Velletri?

Well, if Your Excellency lived in Livorno like us, you would occasionally hear that a small vessel loaded with goods or a nice English yacht, which was expected in Bastia, Porto-Ferrajo, or Civita-Vecchia, has not arrived, that no one knows what has become of it, and that it has probably crashed against some rock.

Well, that rock it encountered is a low and narrow boat, manned by six or eight men, who surprised or plundered it on a dark and stormy night at the turn of some wild and uninhabited islet, just as bandits stop and rob a stagecoach at the edge of a wood.

sentences: The plan for this double kidnapping was therefore set, and it seemed to have every chance of success.

Unless, during the remaining two hours of daylight, it was noticed that the key was missing from the park gate and that the locks had been drawn, Captain Spade and his men were assured of being able to enter the Healthful-House park.
It should be noted, moreover, that, with the exception of Thomas Roch, who was under special surveillance, the other residents of the establishment were not subject to any such measures.
They occupied the pavilions or the rooms of the main buildings located in the upper part of the park.

Everything suggested that Thomas Roch and the guard Gaydon, caught off guard and unable to mount any serious resistance or even call for help, would fall victim to the abduction that Captain Spade was about to attempt on behalf of Count d'Artigas.
Count d'Artigas and Captain Spade boarded the dinghy.
Four oars quickly took them to the schooner, where they climbed up the side ladder.
Count d'Artigas immediately returned to his cabin at the back, while Captain Spade went to the front to give his final orders.
Arriving near the forecastle, he leaned over the starboard rail and searched the water for an object that was floating a few fathoms away.
It was a small buoy, trembling in the ripples of the ebb tide of the Neuze.
Night was gradually falling.
Towards the left bank of the winding river, the indistinct silhouette of New-Berne began to blend into the background.
The houses stood out in black against a horizon still marked by a long streak of fire at the edge of the western clouds.
On the opposite side, the sky faded into some thick vapors.
But it did not seem that rain was to be feared, and these vapors remained in the higher regions of the sky.

Around seven o'clock, the first lights of New-Berne twinkled at various levels of the houses, while the glimmers from the lower quarters reflected in long zigzags, barely flickering just below the banks, as the breeze softened with the evening.

The fishing boats were gently making their way back to the port's coves, some seeking a last breath with their billowing sails, others propelled by their oars, whose sharp and rhythmic strokes spread out into the distance.

Two steamers passed by, shooting jets of sparks from their double smokestacks crowned with black smoke, beating the waters with their powerful paddles, while the machine's balance swung up and down above the spar deck, neighing like a sea monster.

sentences: After dinner, the Count of Monte Cristo was announced.
The young men hadn't seen him for two days.
A matter, Master Pastrini had said, had called him to Civita-Vecchia.
He had left the night before and had only just returned an hour ago.
He had learned that the two friends had wanted to get a box at the Argentina theater, and that he had told them everything was booked.
As a result, he was bringing them the key to his box; at least, that was the apparent reason for his visit.

Franz and Albert hesitated a bit, claiming they were afraid of depriving him of it, but the Count replied that since he was going to the Palli theater that evening, his box at the Argentina would be wasted if they didn't take advantage of it.
Franz had gradually gotten used to the Count's pallor, which had struck him so much the first time he saw him.
He couldn't help but acknowledge the beauty of his stern face, of which the pallor was the only flaw or perhaps the main quality.
A true hero of Byron, Franz could not, we won't say see him, but only think of him without picturing that dark face on Manfred's shoulders or under Lara's cap.

He had that furrow in his forehead which indicates the constant presence of a bitter thought; he had those burning eyes that read deeply into souls; he had that haughty and mocking lip that gives the words that escape it a particular character that makes them deeply engraved in the memory of those who listen.
The Count was no longer young; he was at least forty, and yet it was perfectly clear that he was destined to surpass the young men he would encounter.
In reality, it was that, by a final resemblance to the fantastic heroes of the English poet, the Count seemed to possess the gift of fascination.
Albert was overflowing with happiness about the joy he and Franz had experienced in meeting such a man.
Franz was less enthusiastic, yet he was still under the influence that any superior man exerts on the minds of those around him.

He was thinking about the plan that the Count had already expressed two or three times to go to Paris, and he had no doubt that with his eccentric character, his distinctive face, and his colossal fortune, the Count would make a great impression there.

sentences: That horrifying sight had driven me nearly insane; from the moment I could no longer help anyone, I felt only one need: to flee.
I rushed down the stairs, burying my hands in my hair and letting out a roar of terror.
In the lower room, there were five or six customs officers and two or three gendarmes, a whole armed troop.
They seized me; I didn't even try to resist, I was no longer in control of my senses.
I tried to speak, I let out a few inarticulate cries, that was all.
I saw that the customs officers and gendarmes were pointing at me; I looked down at myself, I was covered in blood.
That warm rain I had felt falling on me through the stairs was the blood of the Carconte.
Then I understood that they were taking me for the murderer.
I regained my voice, I regained my strength; I broke free from the hands of the two men holding me, shouting: "You'll tell your little story to the judges of Nîmes," they replied.
In the meantime, follow us; and if we have one piece of advice for you, it's not to resist.
That was not my intention; I was shattered by astonishment and terror.
They put handcuffs on me, tied me to the tail of a horse, and took me to Nîmes.

I had been followed by a customs officer; he had lost sight of me around the house, suspected I would spend the night there; he had gone to warn his companions, and they arrived just in time to hear the gunshot and to catch me in the midst of such evidence of guilt that I immediately understood how difficult it would be to prove my innocence.
So, I focused on one thing: my first request to the investigating judge was to ask him to search everywhere for a certain Abbé Busoni, who had stopped at the Pont-du-Gard inn during the day.
If Caderousse had made up a story, if this abbé did not exist, it was clear that I was lost, unless Caderousse was caught in turn and confessed everything.
Two months passed during which, I must say in praise of my judge, all efforts were made to find the person I had requested.
I had already lost all hope.
Caderousse had not been caught.

I was about to be tried at the first session when, on September 8, that is, three months and five days after the event, Abbé Busoni, whom I no longer hoped to see, appeared at the jail, saying that he had learned that a prisoner wished to speak to him.
He had learned, he said, about the matter in Marseille, and he was eager to fulfill my request.

Meanwhile, the orchestra's candles were lit; the chandelier descended from the ceiling, casting a sudden cheerfulness into the hall with the sparkle of its facets; then the musicians entered one by one, and at first, there was a long cacophony of rumbling basses, squeaking violins, trumpeting brass, and flutes and piccolos chirping.
But three knocks were heard on the stage; a roll of timpani began, the brass instruments struck chords, and the curtain, rising, revealed a landscape.
It was the crossroads of a wood, with a fountain on the left, shaded by an oak.

Peasants and lords, with their cloaks over their shoulders, sang together a hunting song; then a captain appeared who invoked the angel of evil by raising both arms to the sky; another one showed up; they left; and the hunters resumed.
He had one of those splendid pallors that give something of the majesty of marble to the fiery races of the South.
His strong build was clad in a brown doublet; a small engraved dagger hung at his left thigh, and he rolled his eyes languorously, revealing his white teeth.
It was said that a Polish princess, listening to him sing one evening on the beach of Biarritz, where he was repairing boats, had fallen in love with him.
She had ruined herself because of him.
He had left her for other women; and this sentimental fame only served to enhance his artistic reputation.
The theatrical diplomat even took care to always slip a poetic phrase into the advertisements about the fascination of his person and the sensitivity of his soul.

A beautiful voice, an unflappable poise, more temperament than intelligence and more emphasis than lyricism, further enhanced this admirable charlatan nature, which had something of a hairdresser and a bullfighter.
